target: Je préparais toujours le thé à cinq heures de l'après-midi.
english: I always used to make tea at five in the afternoon.
tip: 'le' shrinks to l' before a vowel: 'le après-midi' becomes 'l'après-midi', the e dropped and joined on.

target: Tu connaissais déjà la réponse quand le professeur a posé la question ?
english: Did you already know the answer when the teacher asked the question?
tip: Two past tenses in one breath: 'connaissais' is the ongoing state (already knew), 'a posé' the single action that happened.
'Jaloux' (m.) → 'jalouse' (f.) = jealous. Adjectives ending in -oux change to -ouse in feminine: doux → douce (exception).
'Mignon' (m.) → 'mignonne' (f.) = cute. Adjectives ending in -on double the 'n' in feminine: bon → bonne, mignon → mignonne.
Mou means soft or squishy: le canapé est mou. It's an oddball – its feminine is molle, not moue.
To say what day it is, French uses 'we are': 'nous sommes lundi' = it's Monday, literally 'we are Monday'.
"Tout va bien" is literally "everything goes well" – French checks how things are with aller (to go), not être (to be). Same verb hides in Comment ça va ?
French makes grooming verbs reflexive: elle se maquille is literally "she makes herself up." The se points the action back on her – no English "herself" needed.
'Pour emporter' = to go / takeaway. 'Sur place' = to eat in. Common at restaurants and cafés.
"Ça ne fait rien" is literally "that does nothing" = no worries / it doesn't matter. The ne...rien pair wraps the verb to mean "nothing."
'Avoir horreur de' = to hate/detest something. An avoir expression: J'ai horreur du lundi = I hate Mondays.
'Salut' is informal for both 'hi' and 'bye'. 'Ça va ?' is the casual way to ask 'how are you?'
Like English 'going to', French uses aller + verb for the near future: 'je vais ... partir' = I'm going to leave.
'Ça fait longtemps' = It's been a while. 'Ça fait + time' expresses duration: Ça fait deux ans = It's been two years.
'Il y a' means 'there is', not 'he has' (that's 'il a'). The y is mandatory: 'il y a du soleil' = it's sunny.
Qu'est-ce qui asks 'what' as the subject, the thing doing the action: qu'est-ce qui s'est passé = what happened. Use qu'est-ce que when 'what' is the object.
Dates use plain numbers where English counts 'fifteenth': 'le quinze mars'. Only the 1st is ordinal – le premier.
Partir uses être: elle est partie. The participle agrees with the feminine subject.
French doesn't "agree" with a verb – you ARE in agreement: être d'accord. Je suis d'accord = literally "I am of agreement."
"dix-huit heures" = 18:00. France runs on the 24-hour clock for schedules, so 6pm becomes eighteen hundred: dix-huit heures, not six heures.

target: Elles ont essayé de nouvelles recettes.
tip: Des shrinks to de when an adjective comes before the noun: de nouvelles recettes, not des nouvelles recettes.

target: Nous avons profité du beau temps.
tip: Profiter de means to make the most of, not just profit: nous avons profité du beau temps = we enjoyed the nice weather. Du is de + le.

target: Elle est montée dans le taxi.
tip: You climb 'into' a vehicle in French: elle est montée dans le taxi = she got into the taxi. Monter takes être here.

target: Il y a beaucoup de monde.
english: There are a lot of people.
tip: 'Il y a' = there is / there are. Works for both singular and plural. 'Il y a du monde' = there are people / it's crowded.

target: Il est cinq heures moins le quart.
tip: "cinq heures moins le quart" is "five hours minus the quarter" = 4:45. Before the hour French subtracts: moins le quart = quarter to.

target: J'ai terminé mes devoirs avant le dîner.
english: I finished my homework before dinner.
tip: Homework is always plural in French: mes devoirs. Le devoir on its own means duty – the plural shifts it to schoolwork.

target: Il a déménagé dans un nouvel appartement.
english: He moved to a new apartment.
tip: Nouveau turns into nouvel before a vowel sound, for smoothness: un nouvel appartement, not un nouveau appartement.

target: Nous avons eu un hiver très froid.
english: We had a very cold winter.
tip: Eu, the past participle of avoir, is pronounced just like the letter u – the e is silent: nous avons eu = we had.

target: Arrête de te plaindre et commence à travailler.
tip: 'Arrête de' + infinitive = stop doing something. 'Commence à' + infinitive = start doing something.

target: Elle a changé de travail le mois dernier.
tip: Changer de takes no article: elle a changé de travail = she changed jobs. It's 'changed of job,' same with changer de train.
